results.claim: Under the recorded definition, an AVL search tree is a Weak Search Tree supporting every insertion and deletion, including rebalancing, in deterministic O(log(n+2)) worst-case time.
results.proof_sketch: Initialize an empty AVL tree. Each node stores a distinct key, two child pointers, and a constant-size balance factor. Maintain (i) the BST invariant and (ii) subtree-height difference at most one. For any node and keys l,r in its left and right subtrees, respectively, the BST invariant gives l<key(node)<r, hence l<r; therefore every maintained tree satisfies the WST invariant. Insert by BST descent and leaf attachment. Delete a node with two children by replacing its key with its inorder successor and deleting that successor; otherwise splice out the node directly. Repair balance bottom-up. At a left-heavy node z, let y be its left child and let A,B,C be y's left subtree, y's right subtree, and z's right subtree. If h(A)>=h(B), right-rotate z; otherwise left-rotate y and then right-rotate z. With a=h(A), b=h(B), c=h(C), imbalance gives 1+max(a,b)=c+2. In the first case a=c+1 and b is c or c+1, which directly verifies both post-rotation balance inequalities. In the second case a=c and b=c+1; the two children of B have heights at most c and differing by at most one, so the double rotation leaves both children of the new root at height c+1. Right-heavy cases are symmetric. Rotations preserve inorder order, hence the BST invariant. There is constant work per ancestor. Finally, the minimum number M(h) of nodes in an AVL tree of height h satisfies M(h)=1+M(h-1)+M(h-2), so M(h)>=2^floor(h/2) and h=O(log(n+2)).

results.claim: For a WST in the standard right-rotation configuration z(left=y(A,B), right=D), the unmodified rotation is a WST exactly when A is empty or every key of A is smaller than key(z); symmetrically, a left rotation at z is safe exactly when D is empty or key(z) is smaller than every key of D.
results.proof_sketch: Before a right rotation, the WST condition at y gives A<B, and the condition at z gives {key(y)}∪A∪B<D, whenever the relevant subtrees are nonempty. After rotation, z has children B,D, so its required comparison B<D is inherited. The new root y has left subtree A and right subtree {key(z)}∪B∪D. Its comparisons A<B and A<D are inherited, leaving exactly A<key(z) as the only new condition. Thus the stated condition is both necessary and sufficient, with A=empty vacuous. For a left rotation, the same calculation with sides exchanged shows that the only new comparison is key(z)<D. Distinct keys exclude equality.

results.claim: There is a three-node WST on which an ordinary right rotation destroys the WST invariant.
results.proof_sketch: Let the root z have key 1 and left child y of key 3, and let y have left child a of key 2; all other children are null. Before rotation, every internal node has an empty right subtree, so every required left-versus-right comparison is vacuous and the tree is a WST. Right-rotating at z makes y the root with left child a and right child z. The WST condition at y would require 2<1, which is false.

results.claim: A three-node WST shows more strongly that permuting only the two pivot keys cannot universally repair a right rotation; a repair retaining the rotated topology may have to touch the transferred subtree.
results.proof_sketch: Take root z=1, its left child y=2, and y's left child a=3, with all other children null. The pre-state is a WST because every internal right subtree is empty. After the right rotation the left leaf has key 3, while the right leaf has one of the two pivot keys. Under either possible permutation of the pivot keys, that right key is 1 or 2, so the root split would require 3<1 or 3<2. Both fail. A valid labeling of the same rotated three-node shape is root 1, left 2, right 3, demonstrating that repair is possible but necessarily moves the key from A. This is the h=0 boundary of the lower-bound family below.

results.claim: The maximum key of a nonempty WST subtree lies among the node keys on the path that follows a nonempty right child and otherwise the left child; in a perfect height-h WST, the h+1 node keys on the right spine can be mutually order-unconstrained by the WST invariant.
results.proof_sketch: At a node with a nonempty right subtree, every left-subtree key is below every right-subtree key, so no left key can be the subtree maximum. The node's own key is unconstrained, hence the maximum is the larger of that key and the maximum found recursively in the right subtree. If the right subtree is empty, recurse into the left subtree instead. For the independence statement, build A_h recursively from a root, a perfect left block L_h, and A_(h-1) on the right. Give successive left blocks disjoint increasing key intervals and put all right-spine root keys in a still larger common interval. Then L_h<A_(h-1) at every level, while no WST split compares an ancestor's stored key with a descendant right-spine root key. Those h+1 candidates may therefore be ordered arbitrarily. Selecting their maximum needs at least h comparisons in the comparison model.

results.claim: In the unaugmented comparison model with only keys and child pointers, an ordinary rotation on a general WST is not a constant-time primitive: for every h>=1 there is an n=2^(h+2)-1 WST at an AVL left-left imbalance for which testing the rotation, and any key-permutation repair that retains the rotated topology, requires Omega(h)=Omega(log n) comparisons in the worst case.
results.proof_sketch: Let A be perfect of height h and B,D perfect of height h-1 (empty when h=0) in z(left=y(A,B),right=D). Then y has height h+1 and z's two child heights differ by two; all proper subtrees are height-balanced, and n=2^(h+2)-1. Assign all A keys below all B keys, all keys in y below all D keys, and leave key(z)=t free as Definition 1 permits. Use the preceding construction so the h+1 right-spine roots of A are independent candidates, all other A keys are below t, and every candidate remains below B. By the rotation characterization, the fixed-key rotation is legal exactly when every candidate is below t. A comparison decision tree must resolve this conjunction, requiring Omega(h) comparisons. For repair, use the subfamily in which both pivot keys are below every A key and all B,D keys are above every A key. In the rotated shape, the root can hide only one low pivot. The other must occupy one of the |A| left positions, forcing at least one original A key outside that block. The root split left<right forces the A keys sent right (or hidden at the root) to include the largest boundary key, or the two largest if the maximum is at the root. Selecting that boundary among h+1 unconstrained candidates also costs Omega(h). The left-rotation statement is symmetric.

results.claim: The rotation lower bound is a precise necessary limitation, not a matching obstruction to the recorded target: it rules out universal constant-time fixed-topology rotation repair without summaries, but not O(log n) updates using a constant number of such repairs, shared work, augmentation, or a nonrotation scheme.
results.proof_sketch: The lower bound is only Omega(log n) for one rotation on a logarithmic-height state, so it is compatible with an O(log n) update if only constantly many independent repaired rotations are needed. Its hypotheses also deliberately fix the rotated topology and exclude cached order summaries. An algorithm might batch several structural changes, maintain extra information if the model permits it, or avoid rotations. Consequently the result sharpens the source's explanation of why ordinary BST rotations do not transfer, but it cannot be promoted into a lower bound against every WST update algorithm.

results.claim: Every valid 2–3 search tree has an explicit one-key-per-binary-node encoding that is a WST; whenever a two-key macro-node occurs, the encoded binary tree is not a strict BST.
results.proof_sketch: Recursively encode each macro-child. A one-key macro-node [a] with ordered children C0,C1 becomes binary node a with left E(C0) and right E(C1). A two-key macro-node [a<b] with children C0,C1,C2, whose key intervals satisfy C0<a<C1<b<C2, becomes root a with right child E(C2) and left child b; node b has children E(C0),E(C1). At b, every left key is below every right key because C0<C1. At a, its left subtree contains b,C0,C1, all of which are below every key of C2. These facts and induction on the macro-height prove the WST invariant at every binary node. If [a<b] occurs, b is a left child of a although b>a, directly violating the strict BST invariant.

results.claim: The encoded macro-node boundaries and search branches are recognizable in constant time per macro level using only keys and child pointers.
results.proof_sketch: At the encoding root a of a one-key macro-node, the left pointer is null at a leaf or enters C0, every key of which is below a. At a two-key macro-node, the left pointer instead reaches the continuation node b>a. Distinct keys therefore let the algorithm distinguish the cases by one structural comparison, without a tag or augmented field. It then uses at most two query-to-macro-key comparisons to select C0, C1, or C2. Thus decoding and routing take at most three key comparisons, hence constant work, per macro level.

results.claim: Insertion into the encoded 2–3 subclass, including every rebalancing split and root-growth case, preserves the encoding using constant work per visited macro level.
results.proof_sketch: Descend by the decoded intervals. A one-key leaf absorbs the new key and becomes a sorted two-key leaf. If a two-key leaf plus the new key gives x<y<z, replace it by one-key leaves [x] and [z] and promote y. When a promoted key enters a one-key parent, that parent becomes a two-key node. When it enters a two-key parent, the resulting three keys x<y<z and four ordered children D0,D1,D2,D3 split into [x] with D0,D1 and [z] with D2,D3, promoting y again. If the old root splits, create root [y] over the two pieces. Each case preserves the search intervals and equal macro-leaf depth. There is at most one split at each ancestor.

results.claim: Deletion from the encoded 2–3 subclass, including every borrow, merge, and root-contraction case, preserves the encoding using constant work per visited macro level.
results.proof_sketch: If the key is internal, replace it by its predecessor from the adjacent child interval and delete that predecessor at a leaf; the interval inequalities remain valid. Removing one key from a two-key leaf leaves a valid one-key leaf. Removing the sole key creates an underfull zero-key macro-node. If an adjacent sibling has two keys, move the intervening parent separator into the underfull node, move the sibling boundary key to the parent, and transfer the boundary child when internal. Both left- and right-borrow cases restore one key per affected node and preserve interval order. Otherwise the sibling has one key: merge the underfull node, separator, and sibling into one two-key node, remove the separator from the parent, and propagate only if the parent underflows. A zero-key root is replaced by its unique child, or by the empty tree. Every repair preserves equal leaf depth and touches only constant-size macro-nodes.

results.claim: An encoded 2–3 tree with n keys has binary height O(log(n+2)), so its search, insertion, deletion, and all associated rebalancing take deterministic O(log(n+2)) worst-case time.
results.proof_sketch: If H is macro-height measured in edges, the minimum key count satisfies N(0)=1 and N(H)=1+2N(H-1), hence N(H)=2^(H+1)-1 and H<=log2(n+1)-1. A one-key macro-node contributes one binary level and a two-key macro-node at most two, so the encoded binary height is at most 2H+1. Decoding and routing take at most three comparisons per macro level. Insertion has one descent followed by at most one constant-size split per ancestor; deletion has at most two descents and one constant-size borrow or merge per ancestor. Root growth or contraction is constant work. All bounds are therefore worst-case, not amortized or expected.

results.claim: The encoded 2–3 construction is genuine non-BST constructive progress and the new rotation theorem is a genuine lower bound, but together they still do not establish logarithmic updates for arbitrary balanced WST states or a matching obstruction under Definition 1 alone.
results.proof_sketch: Encoded states with a two-key macro-node violate strict BST order, yet they satisfy an additional locally recognizable 2–3 parsing, ordered macro intervals, and uniform macro-leaf depth. Definition 1 does not imply those properties, as witnessed by the balanced WST with root 2, left child 3, and right child 4. Conversely, the rotation lower bound applies only to an unaugmented, fixed-topology rotation primitive. No O(log n) conversion or update algorithm for an arbitrary balanced Definition-1 WST has been proved, and no lower bound excludes every possible balancing strategy. This exactly preserves the audit's general-state coverage judgment and supports only PARTIAL resolution.

final_writeup:
Status: partial. The audited encoded 2–3 construction remains a deterministic worst-case logarithmic WST on a genuinely non-BST subclass. The obstruction lens adds a sharp limitation on ordinary rotations, but not a lower bound against every possible WST balancing method.

First, ordinary AVL trees remain a valid baseline: their strict BST invariant implies Definition 1, and their logarithmic height and complete worst-case logarithmic updates follow from the standard balance recurrence. This baseline alone cannot answer the source's weak-only question because it reaches only strict BST states.

The new obstruction can be stated exactly. Write a right-rotation input as z(left=y(A,B),right=D). Before rotation, WST gives A<B at y and {y,A,B}<D at z. Afterwards, the condition B<D at z is inherited. At the new root y, A<B and A<D are inherited, and the only new requirement is A<key(z). Therefore the ordinary right rotation preserves WST if and only if A is empty or max(A)<key(z). Symmetrically, a left rotation is safe if and only if D is empty or key(z)<min(D).

The smallest failure has three nodes. Root 1 with left child 3 and left grandchild 2 is a WST, but its right rotation requires 2<1. An even stronger boundary witness is root 1, left child 2, left grandchild 3: after rotation, permuting only the two pivot keys still leaves key 3 on the left and key 1 or 2 on the right. Thus a universal repair may have to enter the transferred subtree. The empty-A case is safe, while the one-node A case is already enough to force this behavior.

This nonlocality yields a comparison lower bound in the source's unaugmented key-and-pointer representation. In a WST, the maximum of a subtree is among the stored keys encountered by repeatedly following a nonempty right child (or the left child when no right child exists), because the node key itself is not constrained by its children. In a perfect height-H subtree A, the H+1 roots on the right spine can be mutually unordered: attach successively higher ordered left blocks while choosing those root keys independently in a common upper interval.

Embed A as the left child of y in z(left=y(A,B),right=D), with B and D perfect of height H-1. All proper subtrees are height-balanced and z has the exact AVL imbalance two; the total size is 2^(H+2)-1. Choose the surrounding key intervals so the input is a WST and let key(z)=t. The rotation is legal precisely when all H+1 independent candidates in A are below t, which needs Omega(H)=Omega(log n) comparisons without cached summaries. If both pivot keys lie below A and B,D lie above A, any repair retaining the rotated topology must place at least one low pivot in the left block and move a largest-boundary key of A out of it. Selecting that boundary has the same lower bound. This rules out a universal constant-time fixed-topology rotation primitive. It does not rule out a constant number of logarithmic repairs, shared work, augmentation, or nonrotation balancing, so it is not a matching obstruction to the full target.

The constructive progress is unchanged. Encode a one-key 2–3 macro-node [a] as binary node a with its two encoded children. Encode [a<b] as root a with E(C2) on the right and a physical left child b whose children are E(C0),E(C1). Ordered macro intervals prove the WST condition inductively, while b>a on a left edge makes every two-key gadget non-BST. A null left pointer or a left-child comparison with a recognizes the macro arity; one structural comparison plus at most two routing comparisons suffices per macro level.

Standard 2–3 insertion splits an overflow x<y<z into [x] and [z] and promotes y, including root growth. Deletion uses predecessor replacement, borrow from a two-key sibling, merge with a one-key sibling, and root contraction. Each repair changes only a constant-size macro-node and at most one repair propagates per level. A macro-tree of height H has at least 2^(H+1)-1 keys, and each macro-level contributes at most two physical levels. Search and complete insertion and deletion are therefore deterministic O(log(n+2)) worst case.

This family still assumes a locally recognizable 2–3 parse, ordered macro intervals, and uniform macro-leaf depth. Definition 1 alone supplies none of them. No logarithmic conversion or update procedure for an arbitrary balanced WST, and no lower bound covering all possible balancing algorithms, has been established. Under the audit's general-state reading, the open target remains unresolved.
